papers.title: Teaching-learning approaches in homeopathic education: Challenges faced by undergraduate students
papers.abstract: Homeopathic education aims to cultivate competent practitioners through the integration of philosophical principles, clinical reasoning, and experiential learning. However, undergraduate students often encounter significant challenges that influence their academic engagement and professional preparedness. This exploratory review examines prevailing teaching-learning approaches in undergraduate homeopathic education and identifies key challenges perceived by students. Traditional pedagogical models in homeopathy rely heavily on didactic lectures, extensive theoretical instruction, and memorization of Materia medica, which may limit active learning and critical thinking development. Although clinical exposure is emphasized within curricula, inconsistencies in early patient interaction and supervised case-taking affect confidence and skill acquisition. Students also report difficulty in integrating foundational sciences with homeopathic philosophy and clinical application, resulting in fragmented learning experiences. Assessment methods that prioritize recall over analytical reasoning further contribute to academic stress and surface learning tendencies. Faculty-related factors, including variability in teaching competence, limited use of educational technology, and inadequate feedback mechanisms, compound these challenges. Additionally, institutional constraints such as overcrowded classrooms, limited clinical material, and insufficient mentorship hinder personalized learning. This review highlights the need for learner-centered pedagogies, problem-based learning, structured clinical mentoring, and formative assessment strategies to address these issues. By synthesizing existing educational literature and student-centered perspectives, the paper underscores gaps between curricular intent and learning outcomes in undergraduate homeopathic education. The findings suggest that pedagogical reforms focusing on integration, reflection, and competency-based training may enhance student satisfaction and professional readiness. Understanding these challenges is essential for educators and policymakers seeking to strengthen homeopathic education and ensure the development of reflective, confident, and clinically competent graduates capable of meeting contemporary healthcare demands.

papers.title: The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health status of undergraduate medical students in a tertiary care centre in Puducherry: A descriptive cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Abstract Introduction: COVID-19 (coronavirus infectious disease-19), an emerging respiratory disease, was first reported in early December 2019 in the wholesale food market in Wuhan city, China. It had many after effects that affected everyone, but it particularly affected the medical students who could not be certified as medical graduates due to inability to acquire completion of certain certifiable skills. They could not learn the required skills without attending the hospitals. Hence, it caused anxiety and stress among them. The aim of this study was to assess the level of anxiety and stress among the medical undergraduates using two scales. Material and Methods: This was a descriptive cross-sectional study focused on analyzing the mental health of the medical undergraduates using scales, namely the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) scale and the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS). The quantitative data were presented as mean with standard deviation and qualitative data frequency with percentage. Results: Among the study population, 70% were in the age group of 18–21 years, and of them, 58.3% were male and 41.7% were female. The GAD-7 showed a distribution of mild anxiety in 70%, moderate anxiety in 26%, and severe anxiety in 4% of the students. The PSS showed a distribution of 81.9% in the low-stress group and 18% in the moderate-stress group. About 2.8% of the students tested positive for COVID-19, and 35.4% of the students were quarantined due to contact history. About 58.3% of the students were worried about the crisis, and 50.7% of the students stated that virtual classroom is ineffective for learning medical education. Conclusion: Four percent of the students had severe anxiety, and it could be addressed by personalized counseling sessions and reinforcement activities to help students to cope with the anxiety. Students’ welfare committee can be involved in providing counselling services and take necessary steps to involve students in active learning.

papers.title: Beyond Memorisation: Investigating the Influence of Open Inquiry on Chemistry Students’ Scientific Process Skills
papers.abstract: The demand for 21st-century skills, particularly critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific literacy, has necessitated a shift from traditional teacher-centred instruction to student-driven, inquiry-based learning. Open inquiry instructional strategy has been increasingly recognised for its potential to enhance students’ engagement and acquisition of process skills in science education. However, limited empirical evidence exists regarding its effectiveness in contexts where traditional methods still dominate. This study examined the effect of the open inquiry instructional strategy on the development of process skills in chemistry among secondary school students. A quasi-experimental research design was employed, involving a pre-test and post-test with a non-equivalent control group of 322 Senior Secondary School 1 (SSS1) students from six selected schools. Data were collected using the Chemistry Process Skills Assessment Test (CPSAT) and analysed using Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA). The results revealed that students taught using open inquiry performed significantly better in process skills acquisition than those taught using the demonstration method (F(1, 319) = 74.305, p < .001, η² = .189). Additionally, while private school students had slightly higher mean scores than their public school counterparts, the difference was not statistically significant (F(1, 319) = 0.823, p = .365), suggesting that open inquiry is effective across different educational contexts. These findings highlight the need to integrate open inquiry into science curricula to promote active learning. The study recommends incorporating open inquiry into science curricula, providing teachers with targeted professional development, ensuring adequate laboratory resources, adopting a blended instructional approach, offering ongoing teacher support and mentorship, and conducting further research to explore its long-term impact and optimise its implementation.

papers.title: Dual-phase Coexisting Structure of Crystalline Nickel Shell Combined with the Amorphous Copper Prussian Blue Analogue (CuHCF) Core
papers.abstract: In general, when ferricyanide and copper compounds are employed as precursors in the synthesis of copper hexacyanoferrate (CuHCF), the reaction tends to proceed rapidly, often resulting in products with poor crystallinity. The swift reaction rate can cause the CuHCF nanoparticles to form irregularly, thereby preventing the manifestation of the material's intrinsic properties [1]. To address this, we synthesized a complex precursor comprising a chelating agent and copper ions, which was then used to chelate ferricyanide, enabling a more controlled and stable synthesis of CuHCF. Chelating agents such as EDTA are commonly employed for the adsorption of heavy metal ions, including copper. In this study, we utilized the chelating properties of EDTA to achieve the stable synthesis of CuHCF [2, 3]. The resulting CuHCF nanoparticles were not annealed, and the surface retained COOH- groups with a negative potential, which facilitated the reduction of metals on the CuHCF surface. A 0.5 mM solution of EDTA and 0.5 mM copper chloride were co-stirred for 1 hour to form 0.5 L of a pale blue composite aqueous solution. Simultaneously, a 0.5 mM aqueous solution of K4Fe(CN)₆ was prepared. The 0.5 L EDTA-copper chloride composite solution was mixed with 0.5 L of the K4Fe(CN)₆ solution and undisturbed for 24 hours to allow the CuHCF nanocrystals to grow calmly and orderly manner to the lattice structure. The CuHCF nanocrystals were subsequently separated using ultracentrifugation and purified with alcohol to remove impurities. The product was dried using a lyophilizer to obtain CuHCF nanocrystal specimens. Subsequently, a nickel layer was deposited on the surface of the CuHCF to form a dual-phase, core-shell structure. To achieve this, a 0.5 mM solution of nickel chloride hexahydrate (NiCl2·6H2O) was added to the dispersed CuHCF crystals, aged for 3 hours, and the centrifugation and drying processes were repeated. The particle size and surface potential were characterized using a Zeta sizer and Zeta potential measurements, respectively. The crystalline CuHCF had a size of 80 nm and a surface potential of -50 mV, while the crystalline CuHCF/Ni had a size of 100 nm and a surface potential of -30 mV. These results indicate the successful formation of the core-shell structure, leading to an increase in volume. The COOH- groups on the surface of the CuHCF combined with Ni²+ ions and were reduced to nickel metal, resulting in a surface potential change from -50 mV to -30 mV [4]. papers.title: Effectiveness of SWAYAM MOOCs in Bridging Skill Gaps in Undergraduate Education
papers.abstract: How well can massive open online courses close the gap between what universities teach and what employers want? This research examined the effectiveness of SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) MOOCs in addressing skill deficits among undergraduate students enrolled in three institutions. A quasi-experimental pre-test post-test design was adopted with 386 participants selected through stratified random sampling across academic disciplines, gender groups, and urban-rural backgrounds. The Skill Competency Assessment Battery (SCAB), a researcher-developed instrument with established reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.87), measured five core domains: digital literacy, critical thinking, communication, technical proficiency, and problem solving. Each domain contained ten items scored on a five-point rating scale. Participants completed four carefully selected SWAYAM courses over a 16-week intervention period spanning January to April 2024, with weekly institutional mentorship sessions supporting their progress. Results indicated statistically significant improvements across all five skill domains (p < 0.001), with the largest gains observed in digital literacy (Cohen's d = 0.94) and technical skills (Cohen's d = 0.89). The overall mean competency score rose from 40.12 to 64.48, representing a gain of 24.36 percentage points. Critical thinking showed the smallest though still large effect (d = 0.76). Completion rates showed steady improvement over six semesters, climbing from 41.2% in early 2021 to 71.3% by late 2023, substantially exceeding global MOOC averages. Female participants and those from rural backgrounds demonstrated marginally higher skill gains compared to their counterparts, though group differences weren't statistically significant on ANCOVA. Feedback data revealed that 78.3% of participants rated courses as useful or very useful, while inconsistent internet connectivity (34.7%) and balancing MOOC workload with regular coursework (28.9%) were the most commonly reported barriers. The findings suggest that SWAYAM MOOCs serve as an effective supplementary mechanism for skill development in undergraduate education, particularly when embedded within institutional support structures including dedicated mentorship and progress monitoring.

papers.title: Exploring the Chemical and Structural Complexity of Far-From-Equilibrium Oxi-Carbo-Nitride Nanoprecipitates in Additively Manufactured Steels
papers.abstract: Selective laser melting (SLM), a powder bed fusion additive manufacturing (AM) technique, utilizes a high-power laser to selectively melt and fuse metal powders layer-by-layer, enabling far-from-equilibrium micro-/nano-structures, unattainable via conventional manufacturing [1]. The inherent large surface-to-volume ratio of the powder feedstock, produced through inert gas atomization, increases susceptibility to oxygen and nitrogen contaminants. Gas-atomized steel powders typically contain ∼200 wt. ppm (∼700 at. ppm) oxygen and, depending on processing conditions, nitrogen concentrations as high as ∼1000 wt. ppm (∼4000 at. ppm). Due to the low solubility of oxygen in iron, it predominantly forms oxide phases with oxygen-gettering elements present in a steel, such as Si, Mn, Mg, Zr, Al, and Ti. The presence of macro-scale oxide inclusions is of significant concern, as they can deteriorate mechanical properties due to weak cohesion at metal/inclusion heterophase interfaces. While oxygen levels are strictly controlled (<20 wt. ppm) in conventional manufacturing, the inevitably higher oxygen content in AM powders raises concerns about its impact on mechanical performance. Additionally, the residual nitrogen present in the powder feedstock is usually retained in steels after processing, which significantly influences phase stability, microstructure, and mechanical properties, further complicating AM processing. Effective mitigation strategies involve alloying with strong nitride-forming elements, such as Ti and Nb to de-nitride AM microstructures. Recently, QuesTek Innovations LLC developed QT17-4+, a stainless steel specifically designed for AM, based on modifications made to a conventional precipitation-hardened 17-4PH steel. Prior investigations indicate that this martensitic stainless steel demonstrates relatively consistent microstructures and good mechanical properties when processed additively using a wide range of processing parameters and impurity concentrations [2]. The formation of complex O- and N-rich nanoprecipitates was confirmed within the matrix. In this study, we leverage three-dimensional atom-probe tomography (3D-APT) and four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) to elucidate the formation of structurally and chemically complex metastable nanoprecipitates in QT17-4+ for SLM solidification conditions. While 3D-APT provides sub-nanoscale structural and chemical insights, 4D-STEM offers detailed crystallographic information at near-atomic length scales, enabling a comprehensive understanding of nanostructure. Furthermore, we assess whether these nanoprecipitates exhibit partial or complete crystallinity or are amorphous, as their structure directly influences cohesive energies at heterophase interfaces and their impacts on mechanical properties. QT17-4+ steel powders were produced by argon gas atomization and processed using SLM in an argon environment with less than 0.2 vol.% oxygen. The SLM process was performed on a commercial DMG MORI LASERTEC 12 SLM (LT 12 SLM) machine (DMG MORI, Bielefeld, DE) after determining the optimal processing parameters. Focused ion beam (FIB)-prepared lamellas of the 3D-printed specimens were studied employing an energy filtered 4D-STEM (EF-4D-STEM) approach with a near-parallel electron probe (convergence angle of 0.75 mrad) using a JEOL ARM300F(S)TEM equipped with a Gatan Imaging Filter (GIF) Continuum spectrometer coupled to a K3 IS direct electron detector. The open-source py4DSTEM software package was employed for 4D-STEM data analyses [3]. Nanotips for APT investigations were prepared by cutting ∼0.3×0.3×10 mm3 blanks from the SLM-processed specimens, followed by a two-step electropolishing technique [4]. 3D-APT experiments were performed utilizing a laser-pulsed local-electrode atom-probe LEAP5000XS tomograph (Cameca Instruments Inc., Madison, WI) at a base temperature of 60 K in ultrahigh vacuum (<10-8 Pa). Picosecond ultraviolet (UV) laser pulses (wavelength = 355 nm) were applied with an energy of 30 pJ per pulse and a pulse repetition rate of 500 kHz, while maintaining an average detection rate of 2-6%. Data analyses were performed using the program IVAS 3.8.2 (Cameca, Madison, WI). LEAP tomographic datasets were reconstructed using the voltage model. Typical for an auto-tempered martensitic structure, carbon-rich features (predominantly carbon-decorated dislocations and inter-lath boundaries, or epsilon carbides) are often observed in the as-printed steel, Fig. 1. Additionally, our APT analyses reveal the formation of "Ti/Al-oxy-carbo-nitride" nanoprecipitates (D ∼ 20-30 nm) exhibiting a complex core-shell morphology, Fig. 2a. 4DSTEM analyses suggest that these complex nanoprecipitates are made of smaller crystals (D ∼ 2-5 nm), mainly of Al-rich and Ti-rich phases. These nanoscale oxy-carbo-nitrides remove oxygen and nitrogen impurities introduced during the atomization and printing processes from the matrix. Creating an inventory of these micro/nano-structural features is of great interest as it enables us to understand the solidification paths, phase transformations and strengthening mechanisms, as well as identifying potential hydrogen trapping sites within the far-from-equilibrium microstructures [5]. 3D-APT reconstructions of an SLM-processed QT17-4+ stainless steel (Fe-14Cr-5Ni-0.17C-0.5W-0.08V-0.16Ti, wt.%), displaying the distribution of elements within the nanostructure. A total of 310 M atoms is collected in this dataset utilizing a LEAP 5000XS tomograph. For the structures of the Ti- and N- rich features see Fig. 2. (a) 3D-APT reconstruction of a structurally and chemically complex Ti/Al-oxy-carbo-nitride nanoprecipitate formed in an SLM-processed QT17-4+ steel. Four different isoconcentration surfaces are used to reveal the chemical complexity of this nanoprecipitate. These nanoprecipitates form during solidification, effectively de-oxidizing, and de-nitriding the melt pool leading to a more reliable microstructure and improved mechanical properties. (b) 4D-STEM analyses of a similar Ti/Al-Oxy-Carbo-Nitride nanoprecipitate in the same steel, displaying virtual bright-field, annular dark-field, and two different dark-field micrographs reconstructed using the py4DSTEM software package. The dark-field I is reconstructed from the Bragg reflections of a corundum (Al2O3) phase, while dark-field II is reconstructed from the reflections of a phase best indexed as cubic Ti(C,N).

papers.title: Effects of Heat Treatment on the Microstructural Morphology of Additively Manufactured 316L Stainless Steel
papers.abstract: 316L Stainless steel (SS) is widely utilized across various industries, particularly in corrosive environments such as marine, chemical, biomedical, and nuclear energy sectors. In recent years, selective laser melting (SLM) has been increasingly employed to fabricate structural components with complex geometries, enhanced mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance [1]. SLM is a powder bed fusion method that utilizes lasers to selectively fuse powdered materials within a confined chamber [2]. The aim of this research is to study the effects of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical properties of selective laser melted (SLMed) 316L stainless steel with time and temperature. In this study, a SLM 125 3D-printer was used to fabricate 316L SS square plates in a 90 ° build orientation. Specimens were then extracted from these plates and subjected to various tests. These specimens were subjected to varying heat treatments using a Thermcraft XSB box furnace at 600 °C for 2 hours (HT1), 600 °C for 6 hours (HT2), and 850 °C for 2 hours (HT3). After heat treatment, the specimens were cooled in an ambient environment. A LECO LM 100 micro-hardness tester with an applied force of 0.2 kgf for 30 s was used to carry out Vickers hardness testing on metallographically prepared samples which were extracted from the Z-plane. The diagonals of the indentations generated by the micro-hardness tester were measured to calculate the hardness of specimens subjected to each heat treatment as well as the as-printed (AP) specimen. Vertical (parallel to build orientation) and horizontal (perpendicular to build orientation) rectangular specimens were extracted from the 3D-printed 316L SS plates. These specimens had average dimensions of 2.78 mm in thickness, 11.52 mm in width, and 50.80 mm in gauge length. An 810-material test system (MTS) was used to carry out tensile testing on these samples. For the microstructural analysis, samples were taken from as-printed and heat-treated specimens in the XY (top down view) and Z (side view) plane. These samples were metallographically prepared, etched with aqua regia (3:1 mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid), and analyzed with an Olympus DSX 1000 Digital Microscope. A Hitachi S3400N scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to examine the specimens subjected to microhardness testing, and they were also metallographically prepared and etched with aqua regia solution. Table 1 presents the average mechanical properties of the four (4) specimen types (AP, HT1, HT2, HT3) that were tested. From this table the hardness of the specimens can be observed. The HT1 specimen exhibits the highest hardness value of 261 HV, which shows a slight increase compared to the AP specimen. It is also evident that there is a gradual decrease in hardness from HT1 with time and temperature, with HT3 having the lowest hardness value of 211 HV. Similar trends have been reported [3, 4], where heat-treated specimens exhibit an increase in hardness at temperatures up to approximately 600 °C, followed by a gradual decline as temperature increases further. Fig. 1 depicts the SEM analysis of the hardness specimens. The analysis provided insight into their properties, primarily due to the influence of the microstructure and internal stresses on the hardness of SLMed 316L SS [3]. Fig. 1(a) shows the cellular microstructure of the AP specimen, which is typically found in SLMed alloys such as stainless steel, and it is formed due to the rapid cooling rates during solidification. The presence of these cellular structures contributes to the enhanced strength and hardness of SLMed 316L SS [5]. This explains why the AP and HT1 specimens have the highest hardness values as they display a dense cellular structure. The slightly higher hardness value for HT1 can be due its cellular structure appearing to be finer and more uniform. In contrast, the lower hardness value of HT2 can be attributed to the reduced density of its cellular structure resulting from the extended heat-treatment dwell time, as shown in Fig. 1(c). HT3 exhibits the lowest hardness because its cellular structure was completely dissolved at the elevated temperature of 850 °C. Additionally, pores were visible in this specimen, which may have contributed to the low hardness value, as shown in Fig. 1(d). In Table 1, similar to the hardness specimens, the tensile HT1 specimens demonstrated the highest ultimate tensile strength (UTS) values among all specimen types. Notably, the horizontal HT1 specimens displayed a higher UTS than their vertically oriented counterparts, having an average UTS of approximately 663.37 MPa. In contrast, HT2 specimens demonstrated the lowest UTS values, with the vertical HT2 specimens having an average UTS value of approximately 608.8 MPa. HT3 specimens had the highest elongation among all the specimens with a value of about 59.63 % in the vertical orientation. In Fig. 2, optical micrographs of each type of specimen are observed from different perspectives (XY and Z). Specimens analyzed in the XY orientation demonstrated long melt pools that were generated from the laser movement, while specimens in the Z orientation demonstrated overlapping melt pools that have a “fish scale” appearance. Melt pools contribute to the dislocation network of SLMed 316L SS, which strengthens the material; however, with increased temperatures, the dislocation density is reduced [6]. Melt pools can be observed in all specimen types except in HT3 specimens. The melt pools were dissolved as a result of the increased heat-treatment temperature of 850 °C as shown in Fig. 2(d and h). Due to not having any melt pools, the strength of the HT3 specimens was reduced, in turn increasing its elongation. In the HT2 specimens, the extended dwell time of 6 hours decreased the density of melt pools while increasing their size. This resulted in having the lowest UTS values among the tested specimens. papers.title: Real-Time Image Analysis in Microscopy: A Reward-Based Workflow Approach
papers.abstract: Real-time image analysis in STEM and AFM is essential for uncovering the physical and chemical properties of materials, enabling informed decision-making, and advancing experimental workflows [1, 2]. Automated imaging tools increasingly require unsupervised methods that optimize data representation for human interpretation or autonomous experimentation, as classical and neural network-based methods often depend on human input, such as hyperparameter tuning or data labelling [3]. Reward-based workflows address this challenge by framing image analysis as a decision-making process guided by reward functions, enabling robust, explainable, and adaptive optimization [4]. In this study, these workflows were applied to real-time STEM and AFM imaging, achieving effective segmentation, feature extraction, and clustering [5]. By leveraging human decision-making principles, the framework dynamically explores operational spaces, ensuring scalability, robustness, and explainability across a variety of imaging tasks. As an example, the reward approach workflow been implemented to identify amorphous regions within a High-Angle Annular Dark Field (HAADF) image caused by ion irradiation, where real-time detection of amorphous regions requires a physics-informed approach to ensure accurate and adaptive analysis. Clustering techniques, such as Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) [6], rely on pre-set parameters that may not generalize across different experimental conditions, making it challenging to reliably detect structural deviations. To achieve this goal, two key competing metrics have been introduced to guide the optimization: (i) Compactness, ensures that detected regions form well-defined, tightly grouped clusters, while minimizing (ii) Perimeter helps keep structural deviations confined to localized areas. Using Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization problem (MOBO) [7]. the workflow continuously refines GMM hyperparameters based on real-time imaging data, enabling an autonomous exploration of amorphous regions. The parameter space includes descriptor size (wh, ww), which defines the spatial analysis range, and covariance type, which influences variance representation in GMM clustering. As shown in Figure 1, the optimization process identified a balance between objectives, allowing the selection of optimal descriptor size and covariance type using the optimum pareto frontier solution. Reward-based workflows naturally align with Human-Augmented Experimentation (HAE) by allowing researchers to dynamically adjust reward structures in real time. This flexibility enables researchers to modify objectives based on evolving experimental needs, such as prioritizing precision over detection quantity or vice versa. For instance, in a reward-based atom detection workflow (Laplacian of Gaussian)[8] as presented in Figure 2, a researcher can adjust rewards mid-experiment to emphasize higher precision in atomic position prediction (reducing false positives) or increase the number of detected atoms (accepting more false positives). Additionally, HAE workflows facilitate interaction with Pareto Fronts in multi-objective optimization, allowing researchers to select trade-offs that best align with their goals, such as balancing detection accuracy and completeness. This human-in-the-loop approach combines expert judgment with automated optimization, enabling more adaptive, efficient, and context-aware experimentation while maintaining control over the decision-making process [9]. A) GMM clusters based on only one type of Ba atoms, introducing some variety, which it can be differentiated by different values of descriptor size and covariance type in GMM clustering, B) Pareto Frontier solutions with respect to reward possession by MOBO for GMM hyperparameters, and C) Uncovered amorphous areas in the substrate, D) Amorphous regions detection workflow [4]. The left plot presents a Pareto front, demonstrating the trade-off between Objective 1 (precision) and Objective 2 (quantity). The right images showcase how adjusting reward structures can shift the balance, prioritizing higher precision (subplot 1) or increasing the number of detected predictions (subplot 2). This real-time adaptability allows researchers to optimize trade-offs based on experimental goals [5].

papers.title: Investigation of Structural and Magnetic Properties of Mn3Ge Thin Film by Advanced Microscopy
papers.abstract: The non-collinear antiferromagnet Mn3Ge has gained significant attention due to its exotic topological and magnetic properties, making it a promising candidate for next-generation spintronic applications. Its Kagome lattice structure gives rise to anomalous transport phenomena, including a large anomalous Hall effect (AHE) even in the absence of net magnetisation [1]. While bulk Mn3Ge has been extensively studied, its thin-film counterpart remains relatively unexplored. In particular, the relationship between crystallographic phase variations and ferromagnetic behaviour at the Mn3Ge interface requires further investigation. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) provides a high spatial resolution to examine the microstructure, composition, and phase-dependent magnetic properties of Mn3Ge thin films [2]. Furthermore, electron magnetic circular dichroism (EMCD) is employed to directly probe the element-specific magnetic moments of different phases [3-5], combining magnetic force microscopy (MFM) [6] and Lorentz differential phase contrast (LDPC) images provide new insights into their electronic and magnetic configurations. Epitaxial Mn3Ge thin films were grown on (0001) Ru layers on oriented sapphire with an alumina substrate using magnetron sputtering at varying deposition temperatures to stabilise different crystallographic phases. The structural evolution was controlled by adjusting the growth temperature and subsequent annealing conditions, leading to the formation of distinct Mn3Ge polymorphs, including tetragonal and hexagonal phases. STEM was employed to characterize the atomic-scale structure of the Mn3Ge films. High-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) imaging enabled the visualisation of grain boundaries and phase interfaces, while EDX-STEM mapping provided detailed elemental distributions, ensuring homogeneity and composition control. MFM was used to directly probe the nanoscale magnetic domains of the Mn3Ge films, revealing domain configurations unique to each crystallographic phase. The key innovation of this study lies in the application of EMCD to quantify the spin and orbital magnetic moments at an atomic scale. EMCD spectra were obtained in diffraction conditions optimised for Mn L2,3 edges, allowing for phase-resolved magnetic moment extraction. This technique provided critical insight into the variation of magnetic anisotropy and spin polarisation across different Mn3Ge phases. STEM and XRD analysis confirmed the coexistence of hexagonal and tetragonal Mn3Ge phases, with a strong correlation between growth temperature and phase stability. EDX-STEM demonstrated uniform Mn and Ge distributions, ruling out significant chemical segregation. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the structural, compositional, and magnetic properties of Mn3Ge thin films. The application of EMCD to directly probe phase-specific magnetic moments represents a significant advancement in the field of antiferromagnetic spintronics. papers.title: Physico-mechanical characterization of 3D-printed PLGA for patient-specific resorbable implants in craniofacial surgery
papers.abstract: Patient-specific implant (PSI) has optimized the management for a wide range of complex craniofacial deformity over the past years by increasing the accuracy of surgical procedures and lowering the operating time. In hypertelorism (HTO) surgery particularly, the orbital bone repositioning is nowadays guided by patient-specific bone fixation plates that are usually made from non-resorbable alloplastic material (e.g., titanium). Developing resorbable personalized plates could be a relevant alternative to overcome the well-known drawbacks of titanium plates such as infection, exposure or even the lack of bone growth which is detrimental in pediatric patients. This study investigated the mechanical and structural characteristics of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) PSI as resorbable materials for HTO surgery. We assessed the feasibility of printing PLGA PSI by Fused Deposition Modeling additive manufacturing (FDM). The geometrical and the mechanical properties of the 3D-printed device were compared with standard resorbable plates and analyzed after sterilization process (i.e., hydrogen peroxide gas plasma). The Young's modulus was greater than the standard resorbable plates while a decrease of 36% (p = 0.004) after the sterilization was observed. The sterilization also induced a plate deformation with an increase of 0.27 mm in Z-axis and a decrease of 0.8 mm in Y-axis due to annealing effect. Compared to the design, the PLGA PSI were successfully 3D-printed with a maximum deviation of 0.1 mm, making our custom-made plate promising for personalized craniofacial applications. Further investigations on the sterilization process must be considered in view of its mechanical and structural impact on resorbable PSI.

papers.title: An insight into real-time monitoring and predictive modelling of ultrafiltration pretreatment for flow rate and fouling mitigation in seawater desalination
papers.abstract: The growing demand for freshwater, driven by population growth, industrialization, and climate change, has increased global reliance on seawater desalination. While reverse osmosis (RO) remains the primary technology for salt removal, ultrafiltration (UF) plays a critical role as a pretreatment stage by reducing suspended solids, colloids, and microorganisms contributing to RO membrane fouling. This study focuses exclusively on the predictive modelling and real-time optimization of a UF system operating as a pretreatment component in a seawater desalination plant. Using 426 days of operational data, four Machine learning (ML) models: Tree Regression (TR), Ensemble Learning (ENS), Neural Networks (NN), and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) were trained to predict UF flow rates and membrane resistance in real time. ENS achieved the best performance with an R² of 0.99 and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 3.08 L/min, closely followed by TR (R² = 0.99, RMSE = 3.27 L/min). NN and GPR yielded R² of 0.98 (RMSE = 4.69 L/min) and R² of 0.97 (RMSE = 5.98 L/min), respectively. Adaptive backwash control guided by these predictions reduced average TMP excursions by 18 % and decreased backwash frequency from one event every 6 h to one every 8 h, improving operational stability and cutting maintenance costs by 12 %. This framework presents a scalable, intelligent approach to fouling mitigation in seawater desalination pretreatment. • Effects of time, temperature, pressure, pH, and ORP on ultrafiltration performance were investigated. • Ensemble learning and tree regression predicted flow rate with R² = 0.99 and RMSE = 3.08 L/min. • A 426-day seawater UF dataset enabled robust long-term model training and validation. • Real-time sensors improved fouling detection, backwash timing, and energy efficiency. • The ML framework allowed adaptive control of TMP and flow rate, scalable to other membrane systems.

papers.title: Design of an iterative model incorporating transformer-based self-attention and proximal policy optimization for solar power systems
papers.abstract: Solar power integration into modern energy systems relies on accurate and adaptive control models, which are variable and uncertain. Traditional models such as ecurrent neural networkd and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks have problems with scalability, prediction accuracy, and computational efficiency. We present an enhanced control framework that combines three promising methods: Transformer-based models with self-attention mechanisms to understand predispositions, proximal policy optimisation for adaptive learning, and BNNs to update the probabilistic forecast. Transformer-based models use self-attention techniques to capture long-range relationships in time series, improving prediction accuracy and scalability. This model parallelizes inputs to reduce training time, making it better for large-scale applications. Empirically, this approach achieves 95 % prediction accuracy on validation data and 20 % faster training time than LSTM models. This works well with proximal policy optimization, an advanced reinforcement learning technique that allows real-time control policy adjustments based on solar power system data. Since maximum power point tracking and proportional-integral-derivative controllers optimize control actions, this actor-critic structure ensures learning stability and dependability. The model includes VARMAX for pre-emption. The system improved global efficiency by 15 % and updated the control strategy in 100 ms. BNNs are neural networks with uncertainty quantification for solar power generation variability management. BNNs provide probabilistic mean and variance predictions with uncertainty intervals, improving resilience and decision-making. The article found that the model covered the uncertainty interval at 90 %, while the typical neural network had a 10 % reduction in breadth. Using such methods, a solar power system control model would be robust, adaptive, and efficient. This comprehensive solution improves real-time accuracy, adaptiveness, and uncertainty handling, enhancing connected-solar load deployment performance and dependability. Интеграция солнечной энергии в современные энергетические системы опирается на точные и адаптивные модели управления, которые изменчивы и неопределенны. Традиционные модели, такие как сети RNN и LSTM, имеют проблемы с масштабируемостью, точностью прогнозирования и экономичностью вычислений. Мы представляем улучшенную структуру управления, которая объединяет три многообещающих метода: модели на основе трансформера с механизмами внутреннего внимания для понимания предрасположенностей, оптимизацию проксимальной политики для адаптивного обучения и байесовские нейронные сети для обновления вероятностного прогноза. Трансформируемые модели, применяющие методы самовнимания для использования долгосрочных временных отношений, повышают точность прогнозирования и масштабируемость. Эта модель распараллеливает входные данные для сокращения времени обучения, что делает ее лучшей для крупномасштабных приложений. Эмпирически этот подход достигает 95 % точности прогнозирования на данных проверки и приводит к уменьшению времени обучения на 20 %, чем модели LSTM. Это хорошо работает с PPO,передовойусиленной методикой обучения, которая позволяет корректировать политику управления в реальном времени на основе данных солнечной энергосистемы. Поскольку контроллеры MPPTиPIDоптимизируют управляющие действия, эта структура субъект–критик обеспечивает стабильность и надежность обучения. Модель включает VARMAx для упреждения. Система повысила глобальную эффективность на 15 % и обновила стратегию управления за 100 мс. BNN—это нейронные сети с количественной оценкой неопределенности для управления изменчивостью генерации солнечной энергии. BNN предоставляют вероятностные прогнозы среднего и дисперсии с интервалами неопределенности, повышая устойчивость и принятие решений. Установлено, что модель охватывает интервал неопределенности на 90 %, в то время как типичная нейронная сеть имеет 10 %-ный охват. При использовании таких методов модель управления солнечной энергосистемой будет надежной, адаптивной и эффективной. Это комплексное решение повышает точность, адаптивность и обработку неопределенности в реальном времени, повышая производительность и надежность развертывания подключенной солнечной нагрузки.

papers.title: JEMA-SINDYc: End-to-end Control using Joint Embedding Multimodal Alignment in Directed Energy Deposition
papers.abstract: Bringing AI models from digital to real-world applications presents significant challenges due to the complexity and variability of physical environments, often leading to unexpected model behaviors. We propose a framework that learns to translate images into control actions by modeling multimodal real-time data and system dynamics. This end-to-end controller offers enhanced explainability and robustness, making it well suited for complex manufacturing processes. This end-to-end framework differs from traditional approaches that rely on manually engineered features by learning complex relationships directly from raw data. Labels are only required during training to define the observable feature to be optimized. This adaptability significantly reduces development time and enhances scalability across varying conditions. This approach was tested in the Directed Energy Deposition (L-DED) process, a laser-based metal additive manufacturing technique that produces near-net-shape parts with exceptional energy efficiency and flexibility in both geometry and material selection. L-DED is inherently complex, involving multiphysics interactions, multiscale phenomena, and dynamic behaviors, which make modeling and optimization difficult. Effective control is crucial to ensure part quality in this dynamic environment. To address these challenges, we introduce Joint Embedding Multimodal Alignment with Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for control (JEMA-SINDYc). It combines an image-based JEMA monitoring model, which predicts the melt pool size using only the on-axis sensor with labels provided by the off-axis camera, and dynamic modeling using SINDYc, which acts as a World Model by capturing system dynamics within the embedding space. Together, these components enable the development of an advanced controller trained via Behavioral Cloning. This approach improves part quality by minimizing porosity and reducing deformation. Thin-walled cylindrical parts were produced to validate and compare this approach with other control strategies, including both open-loop and JEMA-PID. This framework improves the reliability of AI-driven manufacturing and enhances control of complex industrial processes, potentially enabling wider adoption of the process.

papers.title: Electron Ptychography Resolves Individual Atomic Layers in Twisted Super-Moiré
papers.abstract: Twisted moiré systems have attracted considerable attention due to their tunable electronic and optical properties enabled by interlayer coupling modulated by the twist angle, leading to emergent phenomena such as superconductivity, correlated insulating states, and unconventional ferroelectricity [1]. While most studies have focused on small-angle twisted systems, a new supermoiré lattice has been identified near large commensurate twist angles, exhibiting robust periodicity and flat-band engineerability [2]. Unlike conventional moiré lattices formed by simple AA or AB stacking patterns at small twist angles, the supermoiré domains arise from more complex commensurate stacking arrangements, referred to as commensurate rotational faults (CRFs) [3], making their characterization particularly challenging. In this work, we employ multislice electron ptychography [4] to clearly resolve the individual layer structures of bilayer–bilayer twisted WSe2 near the 21.8° commensurate angle, successfully identifying three distinct CRF structures that collectively form the supermoiré lattice. The schematic of electron ptychography is illustrated in Fig. 1a, where a defocused electron probe scans across the bilayer–bilayer WSe2 sample, with each bilayer having an approximate thickness of 1.5 nm. The resulting diffraction patterns are recorded using an electron microscope pixel array detector (EMPAD). In the reconstruction process, multiple mixed-state probe modes [5] are employed to accurately account for the partial coherence of the electron probe, thereby enhancing resolution. Unlike conventional multislice ptychography reconstruction, regularization is omitted to fully distinguish the two independent bilayers with different orientations. As a result, the reconstructed slices clearly separate the top and bottom bilayers, with each slice containing only a single hexagonal lattice of uniform orientation (Fig. 1b-c). By overlapping the two reconstructed slices, the twisted lattice structure is distinctly visualized (Fig. 1d), providing both high lateral resolution and layer-resolved information. To clearly visualize the supermoiré structure, the inverse fast Fourier transform (iFFT) of the first-order FFT spots (inset Fig. 2a), which correspond to the 21.8° moiré frequency, is generated and overlaid with the twisted lattice (Fig. 2a). A representative supermoiré domain, formed by three commensurate rotational faults (CRFs), is labeled with four sublattice exchange odd site centering around W atoms (SEodd_W) located at the corners, and SEeven and SEodd_Se sites appear in the middle of the domain. Zoomed-in images of the three CRFs, along with their corresponding lattice schematics, are presented in Fig. 2b–d, providing a detailed view of the atomic structures. Although the relatively large 21.8° twist angle results in a small moiré wavelength of only 0.86 nm, the supermoiré structure exhibits a significantly larger periodicity of 7.2 nm. This scale is comparable to the wavelength of small twisted angle systems, highlighting the potential of large twisted angle supermoiré lattices for exploring the interplay among band topology, quantum geometry, and moiré superconductivity [6]. (a) Schematic of the multislice electron ptychography on bilayer-bilayer twisted WSe2. (b-c) Decoupled top (b) and bottom (c) layers. Scale bar: 1nm. (d) Twisted lattice image overlapped by the top (red) and bottom (blue) layer. Scale bar: 2nm. (a) Twisted lattice overlapped with the iFFT image. The super moiré domain is labeled with four SEodd_W (yellow) at the corner and SEodd_Se (blue) and SEeven (purple) in the middle. FFT image is inset with the first order spots labeled in orange circles. Scale bar: 2nm. (b-d) Zoomed in images and lattice schematic of the three CRFs. Scale bar: 0.5nm.

papers.title: Quantitative Analysis of Battery Cathode Nanoparticles using 4D-STEM and EELS
papers.abstract: Chemo-mechanical coupling refers to chemical reactions or changes in composition that influence mechanical properties (such as strain, phase transformations, or defect formations) and, conversely, how mechanical forces affect chemical behavior (such as reduction reaction, diffusion, or ion insertions). This phenomenon significantly impacts the behaviors of cathode materials during electrochemical reactions. Conventional X-ray techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) can provide a statistical analysis of crystal structure, chemical composition, and valence state of the elements [1]. However, due to the limitations of X-ray probe size, it is hard to achieve correlative analysis on a single nanoparticle with nanometer resolution. In scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), correlative imaging has been successfully shown to map structural and chemical response upon ion insertion using four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) and electron-energy loss spectroscopy (EELS). While 4D-STEM probes the lattice structure, including structure identification, orientation classification, and strain measurement with nanometer spatial resolution [2], core-loss EELS by calculating the L3/L2 area ratio enables tracking of the valence state of metal ions in cathode nanoparticles [3]. Chen et al. showed local structure heterogeneity of metal oxide cathode nanoparticles significantly influences ion insertion efficiency, leading to the formation of oriented phase domains [4]. In this study, we further develop quantitative 4D-STEM correlated with EELS characterization in 2 nm spatial resolution to study the MnOx cathode nanoparticles discharged in different organic electrolytes. In Mg-ion batteries, common solvents used for electrolytes such as (PhMgCl)2-AlCl3 (APC) have chloride ions involved during the ion insertion process, which causes cathode degradation. Magnesium (II) Bis (trifluoromethane sulfonyl) / Tetrahydrofuran (Mg(TFSI)2/ THF) has good anodic stability that enables the electrochemical reaction work at high voltage conditions, which makes it a promising candidate electrolyte for next-generation multivalence ion batteries [5]. Here, we employ a quantitative 4D-STEM correlated with EELS characterization (Fig. 1) to investigate the cathode MnOx discharged in two different electrolytes: APC/ THF and Mg(TFSI)2/ THF. When comparing their impact on cathode charge-lattice coupling, we found significant differences shown in Figure 2. When MnOx is discharged in APC/ THF electrolyte, strain mapping from 4D-STEM shows that most of the strain occurs on the surface of the particles. Correlative Mn valence state mapping shows that most of the ions are trapped in the surface region. However, when MnOx is discharged in Mg(TFSI)2/ THF, the strain of the surface does not affect the ion insertion, which results in a uniform valence state mapping of Mn. To further understand the structure of cathode nanoparticles, we are working to develop a quantitative 4D-STEM technique that could quantify the structure heterogeneity and defects in the cathode nanoparticles system [6]. papers.title: Formación Docente en IA Generativa: Impacto Ético y Retos en Educación Superior
papers.abstract: La inteligencia artificial generativa (IA-G) está redefiniendo la educación a nivel superior, cambiando los enfoques en la enseñanza y evaluación, y para su integración, los docentes deben desarrollar habilidades técnicas y criterios pedagógicos que les permitan utilizar estas herramientas con conciencia ética. Este estudio analiza el impacto del programa de formación en IA-G de 80 horas impartido a 299 docentes de ocho universidades ecuatorianas, con el propósito de fortalecer sus competencias digitales y su disposición hacia estas tecnologías. Mediante un diseño cuasi-experimental con mediciones pretest y postest, los resultados mostraron mejoría en el conocimiento técnico sobre IA-G (M = 2.62 a 4.22, t = -30.77, p < 0.0001, d = 0.85) y en la predisposición docente para su aplicación en el aula (M = 3.63 a 4.02, t = -6.38, p < 0.0001, d = 0.52). Sin embargo, la percepción sobre la originalidad de los contenidos generados por IA no mostró cambios relevantes (M = 3.02 a 2.94, t = -0.82, p = 0.41), lo que sugiere incertidumbre sobre su autenticidad académica. Estos resultados destacan la importancia de una capacitación que combine instrucción con metodologías activas, como el aprendizaje basado en proyectos y la evaluación formativa. Asimismo, se recomienda establecer políticas institucionales claras sobre el uso de IA en la educación superior, priorizando ética y transparencia acorde con los principios de la UNESCO.//Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) is reshaping on higher education, and transforming instructional and assessment practices, therefore, educators must develop technical expertise and pedagogical awareness to ensure ethical and responsible use. This study evaluates the impact of an 80-hour GAI training program conducted with 299 lecturers from eight Ecuadorian universities, aiming to enhance their digital skills and openness to AI-based teaching strategies. Through a quasi-experimental design with pretest and postest assessments, findings reveal an increase in technical proficiency (M = 2.62 to 4.22, t = -30.77, p < 0.0001, d = 0.85) and lecturers’ willingness to apply GAI in their teaching (M = 3.63 to 4.02, t = -6.38, p < 0.0001, d = 0.52). However, perceptions of AI-generated content originality remained unchanged perceptions (M = 3.02 to 2.94, t = -0.82, p = 0.41), indicating ongoing concerns regarding authenticity in academic settings. These results emphasize the necessity of training programs that merge technical instruction with active learning methodologies, such as project-based learning and formative assessment. Additionally, higher education institutions should establish clear policies regulating AI implementation, ensuring ethical standards and academic integrity. Moreover, developing institutional guidelines for assessing AI-generated content is essential for maintaining transparency, fairness, and responsible adoption in teaching and assessment to identify the best practices to support lecturers’ development, and promote its effective use in academic fields.

papers.title: Identification of Unique Pd-based Compounds in Twisted MoTe2 Nanojunctions
papers.abstract: Introducing superconductivity in topological materials can lead to innovative electronic phases and device functionalities. Recent observations of fractional quantum anomalous Hall effect in twisted bilayer molybdenum ditelluride have confirmed the existence of fractional Chern insulators in the absence of magnetic fields. In principle, the creation of superconductivity in fractional Chern insulators can lead to interesting electronic states of matter under unexplored experimental conditions. However, creating superconductivity using traditional means in such air-sensitive two-dimensional (2D) moiré materials is challenging. [1-6] We overcome such challenges by presenting a unique strategy for constructing high-quality superconducting junctions consisting of air-sensitive van der Waals moiré materials, such as twisted bilayer MoTe2 [1-3]. We present systematic characterizations of the junction, including both the atomic structure and the electronic transport behaviors. The key to our approach to fabricating high-quality superconducting moiré junctions is the recently introduced on-chip 2D growth mechanism based on the unexpected discovery of rapid mass transport, and crystal growth templated on 2D materials [2]. We use this approach to find that a class of unique Pd-based compounds produced on topological chalcogenides are superconductors [1, 2]. Here, we demonstrated atomic-resolution visualization of a complicated compound (Pd7MoTe2) with high crystalline quality by using high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) (no serious beam damage issue [7-9]). Using STEM, we characterize the new compound Pd7MoTe2 and the nanojunction, following the fabrication and experimental procedures described in Refs. [1, 3] for both cross-section and plan-view STEM studies. Figure 1a shows a STEM image of a suspended twisted MoTe2 film placed on a Pd-deposited TEM grid, after the heat treatment at 190°C for 6 min. The lateral growth of the compound (brighter area) from the Pd outer seed leads to a junction of Pd7MoTe2/MoTe2/Pd7MoTe2 where the MoTe2 gap is about 30 nm wide. We performed energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis on the film (Fig. 1b) and confirmed that the atomic ratio of Pd/Mo/Te in the compound is always very close to 7:1:2. Figure 1c displays high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) images with an atomic resolution, which reveals both a crystalline structure of the Pd7MoTe2 and the moiré lattice of twisted bilayer MoTe2. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern of the region twisted MoTe2 (Fig. 1d) confirms its lattice structure as well as a twist angle of 3.7°, which is the target angle during fabrication. It is remarkable that an exceptionally sharp lateral interface (<1 nm) between Pd7MoTe2 and twisted MoTe2 is achieved and that the moiré structure of twisted MoTe2 remains intact in the junction (Fig. 1f). Our gentle and low-temperature growth helps improve and protect the moiré homogeneity because the ultrathin Pd film serves as a glue that seals the two MoTe2 monolayers, an advantage of our approach [10]. STEM analysis of twisted bilayer MoTe2 moiré junction with sharp interfaces. (a) STEM image of twisted MoTe2 after the growth of Pd7MoTe2, prepared on a TEM grid (sample T1). The TEM grid is predeposited with Pd, then transferring MoTe2 on top. Subsequently, Pd is introduced by holding the temperature at 190°C for 6 min, resulting in a twisted MoTe2 moiré junction with a width of approximately 30 nm. Regions of different materials are indicated. (b) HAADF and corresponding elemental mappings captured at the moiré junction. The atomic ratio of Pd:Mo:Te is close to 7:1:2 in the compound as grown, while negligible Pd can be observed in the neighboring twisted MoTe2 area. (c) An atomic-resolution STEM image of the moiré junction. (d) The FFT pattern of the twisted MoTe2 regime confirms the twist angle of 3.7°. (e) The FFT pattern of the crystalline Pd7MoTe2 shows the sixfold symmetry. (f) The magnification of the STEM image at the interface is marked in a red rectangle in (c). The crystalline structures of both Pd7MoTe2 and twisted MoTe2 can be visualized, demonstrating a sharp interface between the two regions. The moiré structure of twisted MoTe2 remains intact.

papers.title: Probing Magnetically Active Intercalant Disorder with Atomic Resolution Imaging and Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have attracted great interest due to their wide range of functional properties which can be tuned with changes in thickness, stacking order, and twist [1]. Introducing intercalants into the van der Waals (vdW) gap of these materials adds a rich new dimension of electrochemical, electronic and magnetic properties [2]. Of particular recent interest is the addition of magnetic intercalants, which can give rise to magnetic behavior useful for spintronics including sharp magnetization switching, chiral textures, and potentially altermagnetism [3-5]. The ability to easily manipualte these systems by altering the intercalant and host lattice structure makes these materials an ideal platform for exploring exchange interactions, magnetic correlations, and spin coupling to lattice and electronic degrees of freedom. However, the large structural configuration space, including the intercalant concentration and site occupation, as well as the composition, stacking sequence, and degree of inhomogeneity of both the intercalants and host lattice, poses a major material design challenge [6]. This complexity and the inevitable presence of disorder in real world samples makes it difficult to disentangle the connections between these structural features and the useful emergent magnetic properties realized in these materials. Here, we study 2H-NbS2, which in its pristine state hosts charge density wave and superconducting phases, intercalated with magnetic vanadium ions [7]. Introducing vanadium to the material results in a wide range of magnetic behavior associated with subtle variations in structural order and disorder extending across length scales. VxNbS2 samples were grown from the constituent elements via chemical vapor transport, with small variations around the target vanadium stoichiometry of x=1/3 measured by energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. These samples exhibit significant variability in magnetic properties not directly correlated with the measured stoichiometric variations, suggesting other structural features might play a major role in governing the magnetic behavior of the material. To study the connection between crystalline symmetry and magnetic properties, selected area electron diffraction (SAED) measurements were performed. Long range order of the intercalants reduce the symmetry of the structure, generating superstructure reflections in the SAED patterns predominantly corresponding to a a √3x√3 superlattice, as expected for this sample composition (Fig. 1b) [8]. In addition to the superlattice peaks, diffuse scattering intensity between the peaks predominantly oriented along the [001] vdW layering direction suggests the presence of stacking disorder. While SAED measurements reveal the ensemble reciprocal space structure of the material, to understand its disorder and inhomogeneity atomic resolution characterization with high-angle annular dark field (HAADF) STEM imaging is needed. HAADF imaging on the [100] axis reveals the coordination and stacking sequence of the TMD layers, while the [110] axis allows the vanadium atomic columns found in the vdW gap comprising the √3x√3 superlattice to be directly resolved. For instance, in the HAADF image in Figure 1c occupation of the three possible octahedral sites in the vdW gap (Fig. 1a) can be seen, with significant disorder disrupting a largely bilayer “AB” alternating stacking sequence. To characterize this disorder, the occupation of each intercalant site can be mapped to reveal clusters of site disorder as well as extended faults in the stacking order (Fig. 1d). While this HAADF characterization clarifies the nature of intercalant site order and disorder in the vdW gap, it is insensitive to another potentially relevant form of disorder: substitution of the transition metal in the TMD layers. To study this, we performed atomic resolution core loss electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) to map out the spatial distribution of each element in the material (Fig. 2a). The vanadium intercalants are easily knocked out of the intercalant sites in the vdW gap, necessitating great care to avoid damage to the structure while acquiring sufficient signal for reliable mapping: here we use a 30 pA probe current and 120 kV accelerating voltage to minimize beam induced effects. Using a Thermo-Fisher Spectra 300 equipped with a high-brightness X-CFEG source, spectrum images including niobium, sulfur and vanadium edges were collected on a Gatan Continuum CMOS detector optimized for low primary energies, allowing the distribution of each element in the TMD and interstitial layers to be resolved (Fig. 2b,c). This elemental mapping and associated fine structure information provides valuable insight into the atomic scale presence of chemical disorder in the material. Correlating diffraction, imaging, and spectroscopy measurements across a range of samples, we assemble a comprehensive picture of intercalant and substitutional disorder from the angstrom to micron length scale, reconciling questions of how vanadium incorporates into the system, alters global symmetries and local coordination environments, and tunes exchange interactions, towards achieving control of the emergent magnetic properties exhibited by the material [9]. Imaging and diffraction of [110] zone VxNbS2. a) A schematic of the material structure showing the TMD layers and three possible octahedral intercalation sites in the vdW gap marked with red, blue, and green circles. Filled and unfilled circles depict the nominal bilayer stacking sequence (unit cell marked by black box) as well as the vacancy and partial occupation of the sites arising from interstitial site disorder and substitutional disorder in the TMD layers. b) A SAED pattern showing superstructure reflections consistent with a bilayer stacked √3x√3 superlattice. Diffuse scattering is visible connecting the peaks along the vertical [001] direction. c) An atomic resolution HAADF-STEM image with resolved TMD layers and vanadium intercalant columns visible in the vdW gap. d) Map of interstitial site occupation (3 sites marked in red, green, and blue) across the same field of view shown in (c). Electron energy loss spectroscopy of the same sample shown in Fig. 1, revealing substitutional disorder. a) Background subtracted niobium, sulfur, and vanadium edges used for mapping. b) simultaneously acquired ADF image corrected for drift, showing the layered material structure on the [110] zone axis. c) EELS intensity profiles showing the distribution of each element in the TMD layers and vdW gap, revealing vanadium substitution onto niobium sites.

papers.title: Microscopy and Microanalysis in Modern Engineering Materials and Additive Manufacturing Education
papers.abstract: The fourth industrial revolution, Industry 4.0 (I4.0), has had a massive impact on Engineering education and its delivery over the last decade. I4.0, which involves the digitisation of manufacturing, has led to the inclusion of topics such as Additive Manufacturing (AM), Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), into university curricula. Industry 5.0 (I5.0), however, is already here and calls for further modernisation of both engineering units and how they may be taught. In contrast to I4.0 which is technology focused, I5.0 stipulates that the implementation of technology needs to be human-centric, resilient and sustainable [1]. In Europe, a key focus for I5.0 has also been identified as achieving the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) [2]. These I5.0 concepts and goals therefore cover not only industry and engineering, but all of society in general. Moving forward, the overarching objective for Engineering Education which covers I4.0 and I5.0 concepts, would therefore be to provide authentic, relevant, creative, student-centred projects that have an integrated, interdisciplinary approach and teach transferrable skills. For example, future jobs in engineering will require workers to be skilled in areas such as bio and nano-inspired materials. In order to meet the UN’s SDGs, there is also a need for new composites and recycled materials. All require advanced knowledge of not only a diverse array of materials and how they interact with each other, but also material analysis techniques and their use in material quality control. Engineers therefore need to be trained using experimental and research based pedagogical strategies when it comes to engineering materials [3]. This is where microscopy and microanalysis can play a large part. Solomon and co-workers found that when microscopy and microanalysis was incorporated into mechanical engineering curriculum, including topics on material crystallinity and material failure analysis, students formed a greater understanding as they got first-hand experience seeing and handling samples [4]. Additive manufacturing is evolving from just prototyping, and into mainstream production due to its ability to produce internally complex parts. Development of new materials (e.g. polymers, metals, resins, ceramics and composites) is also accelerating. including, which undergo processes such as extrusion, softening, melting, fusion and sintering to name a few. In plastic additive manufacturing, new ultra-high-performance polymers such as Ultem, PEEK, PEKK or PPS only gain their full-strength properties when annealed or treated and have drastically different properties based on levels of crystallinity. This can also be affected by additives and fillers, such as glass fibre, carbon fibre, Kevlar, continuous fibres and metal powders. Some of these also provide unique material properties such as conductivity, radiation absorption, thermal conduction and strength. Raw material quality, the production process used and print geometry of the final components all influence the final product. Additive manufacturing is also being investigated as a possible repair technology. For example, Angel and Basak have researched its use in repairing metallic single crystal turbine blades found in aircraft turbo engines [5]. Applications of additive manufacturing in more demanding spaces such as in aerospace, marine, medical and defence has also increased, leading to a greater need for quality control, material certification, extreme tolerances and consistency. The very nature of producing parts layer by layer also opens possibilities for all types of failures, weaknesses and imperfections. Due to the new and diverse array of materials now available, the next generation of engineers must have advanced knowledge not only of their properties, but also their quality. In an additive manufacturing workplace setting, material analysis is essential and ideally needs to be done at the time and place of part production. Results can therefore be quickly fed back into the design and manufacturing process. Education on material characterisation and analysis techniques is therefore critical. Characterisation and quality control of both the initial raw materials is and final products is needed. Manufacturers need to ensure they avoid “garbage in, garbage out” situations. Minor changes in chemical composition between batches of raw material can have significant impact during additive manufacturing production. For example, many 3D printing filament plastics are hydroscopic and therefore absorb water, which affects the quality of a print, while metal powders can oxidise if exposed to air, thereby creating an oxide layer which can cause potential defects during sintering. SEM and FTIR have previously been used to show how UV and thermal exposure can age polymer filaments and printed products [6], while micro-CT of whole polymer filament rolls has been used to show the wide variations which can occur in rolls of the same type of filament, from the same manufacturer [7]. Microscopy and Microanalysis techniques, such SEM, EDS, FTIR, XRD, thermal analysis and micro-CT can be used to fully characterize materials (Table 1). Figures 1-4 provide examples of characterisation techniques that could be utilised to analyse polymer filament for 3D printing. In order to align with I4.0 and I5.0 concepts and practices, discipline boundaries at universities need to overlap [8]. While a fusion of Engineering and Materials Science is common, we are now starting to see university core facilities combine/overlap with Makerspaces, which were once predominantly used in the realm of Engineering studies. Makerspaces allow for the design, prototyping, modelling and fabrication of custom parts. For example, it is becoming common in university core facilities to see staff use CAD programs such as Fusion360 to design and 3D print custom holders for various instruments, tailored to unusual sample shapes and sizes. McCullough and colleagues [9], discuss the idea and design of a Biomanufacturing Maker Lab, which expands on the features of the maker space to include a multidisciplinary approach that now includes biology and biological products (e.g. biorobotics, bioprinting, etc.) and includes a wet-space. A similar direction could be taken by combining a makerspace with materials characterization. This would see the ability for students to not only design and fabricate parts, but do so using new materials, which they can characterise both before and after manufacture. A similar idea has been set up at the University of Pennsylvania [10] with the creation of a MatSci Makerspace. Here, in the one place, university undergraduates have access to materials synthesis and characterization equipment such as SEMs, mechanical and thermal testing. Microscopy and microanalysis of 3D printing filaments provides a great tool to teach engineering students about material parameters in a way that is hands on, creative and iterative. The use of different types of filaments also allows the educators to bring in discussions on I5.0 topics such as material sustainability and SDGs that could be met. In this work we present examples of different materials characterization techniques that could be used. Table 1 explains each technique and what it is used for, while Figures 1-3 provide examples of how each technique can be used to show differences between materials. In conclusion, we show how a polymer 3D printing project can offer an accessible way for students to engage in engineering materials education that covers I4.0/ I5.0 principles, and the major role microscopy and microanalysis can play [11]. From left to right they show a Polylactic acid (PLA) + Steel composite, Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) + carbon fibre composite, and toughened Polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) filament. Each filament was fractured longitudinally after liquid nitrogen freezing. SEM shows the particles/fillers/fibres present in a material and their sizes, while EDS confirms what elements are present. For example here, PPS and PET-CF show black circles which are internal voids in the filament. (Note that different colour scales have been used for each row).
